question: Do I need a condom if I am on the pill?
reply_1: Yes, if you want protection from STIs. Condoms are the only contraceptive method that prevents both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Other methods prevent pregnancy only, so Kenyan guidance strongly encourages young people to use condoms as well, for dual protection.
reply_2: Yes. Kenya's family planning guideline says you can use combined pills, the injection, the implant and the female condom even if you have never had a baby. For the combined pill it lists ages from your first period up to 40 years. A health worker will check which method is right for your age and health.

question: will the injection make me unable to have kids
reply_1: No. WHO states that modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. After you stop a method your fertility comes back, though Kenya's guidelines say that for most methods it can take 3 to 6 months on average. Getting pregnant later is still possible.

question: I have discharge and itching down there, is it an STI?
reply_1: No. Bacterial vaginosis, the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age, is not an STI, and neither is a yeast infection (thrush). Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause a yellow or greenish, sometimes frothy, discharge and itching, and many women who have it have no symptoms. Because these can look alike, you can't tell by yourself. A health worker can test you and tell you which it is.
reply_2: It could be. Unusual discharge, genital sores or lower belly pain can be signs of an STI, but many STIs cause no symptoms at all, so only a test can tell. A health worker can examine you and give treatment, and Kenya's guidelines say providers must ensure privacy and confidentiality when serving adolescents.

question: is it normal for my period to be irregular
reply_1: Light spotting or irregular bleeding is common with both. The guideline says it is common with the injection, especially in the first 6 to 8 months, and with the implant, especially in the first year. It says this is not harmful and usually does not need treatment. If the bleeding keeps going or worries you, see a health worker.
reply_2: In the first years after periods start they are often irregular. WHO says bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful or heavy, or that stops you doing normal activities, could point to an underlying health condition, so see a health worker. A late period can have many causes, including pregnancy.

question: my private parts are burning, what could it be
reply_1: It could be. Kenya's guidelines describe a yeast infection (vaginal candidiasis) as causing itching or burning of the vulva, soreness, and a thick white or creamy discharge that is often like curds. It is not an STI, but its signs look like some STIs, and the same signs can also be caused by other infections, so it needs to be checked. Wet pads can encourage fungal infections like this, so change pads regularly. See a health worker for a test and treatment.

question: Where can I get a pregnancy test
reply_1: The way to find out is a urine pregnancy test. Kenya's guidelines say that when a period is late, irregular or you are not sure, a urine pregnancy test should be done. Ask a health worker or a youth-friendly clinic for one. Until you have a test result, you cannot be sure you are not pregnant. Use a condom or avoid sex until your period comes or the result is confirmed.
reply_2: Under Kenya's 2020 national school re-entry guidelines, a pregnant learner is allowed to stay in school for as long as possible and to sit national exams if her health allows. After delivery she is re-admitted to the same class she was in before. The guidelines give the return time as six months after delivery and also as the start of the next calendar year, so ask your school's guidance and counselling teacher what applies to you.

reply_2: PrEP is medicine that HIV-negative people take to lower their risk of getting HIV. Kenya's 2022 guidelines say it is for sexually active people aged 15 and over who test HIV-negative, and it is available across all 47 counties. A health worker will test you and check it is right for you. PrEP does not protect against other STIs, so condoms still matter.
